# The test files that start a real `go` or `git` command in the unit tier on
# purpose.
#
# internal/testkit/tiers_test.go::TestEveryToolchainDrivingTestIsIntegrationTagged
# reads this file. Every other test file that starts one has to carry
# `//go:build integration`; the ones below are the exceptions, and each is here
# because tagging it would leave a package with no evidence for the one thing it
# exists to do.
#
# The list is a ledger, not a configuration. A stale entry is reported as loudly
# as an offender, so it shrinks when a suite is tagged and grows only when
# somebody writes a path down and says why underneath it.
#
# One path per line, relative to the module root, `/`-separated. `#` comments
# and blank lines are ignored.

# internal/gocmd used to be the first entry here, and it is gone: its unit tier
# scripts a toolchain instead of reaching for one. A version probe that answers
# garbage, one that exits non-zero and one that hangs are all answered now by
# internal/testkit/mutantkit's fake `go` — a real process reading its answers
# from a table — so the wrapper every other package depends on keeps its
# unit-tier evidence and needs no toolchain to produce it. The four claims that
# are about a *real* `go` rather than about go-mutants' own code moved to
# internal/gocmd/toolchain_integration_test.go, which is where they belong.
#
# A fake-driven file is exempt by construction: the scan skips any test file
# that constructs a fake, because a file that supplies the toolchain is not
# reaching for one. That exemption is also why a file may not do both — hence
# the split above — and it is pinned by
# TestAFileThatScriptsTheToolchainIsNotDrivingOne.

# internal/discover loads the fixture modules with go/packages, which drives a
# real toolchain by construction: the questions this package answers — the
# universe's `true` against a shadowed one, a type argument against a map index,
# a cgo file on a machine with cgo switched off — are facts about go/types that
# a fake would have to invent, so there would be nothing left to test behind a
# mock. It is the most expensive entry in this ledger at about five seconds, and
# it is the one whose skip used to be silent: its helper now goes through
# testkit.GoBinary, so a runner that lost its toolchain fails the job instead of
# retiring seventy-four tests and reporting green.
internal/discover/discover_test.go
internal/discover/skipsites_test.go

# internal/instrument generates Go source, and the only claim that matters about
# generated source is that it is a program. These three compile what the
# instrumenter produced — the mutated tree, the probe rewrite, the probe sites —
# and a suite that asserted on the text instead would pass on output no compiler
# accepts. That is the defect class this package has actually shipped.
internal/instrument/compile_test.go
internal/instrument/probe_test.go
internal/instrument/probesites_test.go

# The harness's own tests are the toolchain policy's tests.
#
# internal/testkit is what decides which tools a test may reach, what happens
# when one is missing, and what environment a child `go` command is handed — and
# none of that can be checked without running one. tools_test.go is the policy
# itself: skip without a toolchain, fail under GO_MUTANTS_TEST_REQUIRE_TOOLS,
# and the same for git. env_test.go and module_test.go run a real `go` over a
# composed environment and a synthesized module, because "GOFLAGS reached the
# child" and "this module builds" are claims about a `go` command rather than
# about a []string. tiers_test.go runs the two `go test -list` invocations that
# prove this very tiering.
#
# They are named here rather than exempt by construction, which is why the three
# harness needles are matched unqualified: written as `testkit.GoBinary(` they
# would never match a call from inside package testkit, and the one package
# whose subject is the tier policy would be the one package outside it.
internal/testkit/env_test.go
internal/testkit/module_test.go
internal/testkit/tiers_test.go
internal/testkit/tools_test.go

# internal/sourcegate's pointer-conversion gate type-checks this module, which needs
# a real toolchain by construction: the questions it asks — which package
# `u.Pointer` names under an import alias, whether the `syscall` in
# `syscall.SyscallN` is an import or a local with a method of that name — are
# bindings, and a scan over identifier text is wrong about all of them. It is
# also the one gate that has to see files this platform does not build, so it
# loads the module once for `GOOS=windows` and once for the host: a build
# constraint hides a file from the type checker exactly as it hides it from the
# compiler, and the Windows job object is where the rule was broken.
#
# Tagging it `integration` would retire it from the tier that runs on every
# push, which is the only tier that would catch the conversion being written
# back the wrong way round. About four seconds against a warm build cache.
internal/sourcegate/unsafeptr_test.go
